HOUSTON, Oct 30 : Oil prices jumped more than 2 per cent on Friday and settled at their highest levels since the end of April, as traders braced for a potential escalation in the Iran war after the US midterm elections, with an attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz highlighting supply risks. Brent crude futures for December, which expired on Friday, settled up $2.76, or 2.4 per cent, at $117.64 a barrel, after touching a high of $118. The more active January contract gained $2.63 to $113.43. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures settled $2.12, or 2.08 per cent, higher at $104.12. For the month, Brent finished 13.6 per cent higher, while WTI rose 15.2 per cent.

"Traders will remain focused on oil flows out of the Middle East and the likely escalation by US and allied forces," said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial.  On Friday, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by explosive devices attached by a small boat, said the UKMTO, the British maritime security service. It was not immediately clear who was behind the attack in the strait, the key sea outlet for Gulf crude and fuel supplies.  It was the first known successful strike in the waterway using limpet mines, explosives that are attached to a ship's hull from a small boat, since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, maritime sources said. 'HIGHER LIKELIHOOD OF AN ESCALATION' The US ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia effective October 23 due to safety risks, the US embassy in Riyadh said on Friday, citing Houthi attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure. Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi militants said on Thursday they had attacked several sites in Saudi Arabia, including the large Ras Tanura oil refinery, the Rabigh refinery and a production facility in Abqaiq owned by state oil company Saudi Aramco.  A Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted a cruise missile launched by the Houthis towards the kingdom's western region. Meanwhile, Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of coordinated efforts to reach a deal between the US and Iran, an official briefed on the talks told Reuters. US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Iran to help the country get medical supplies, after US media reported Vance had written to Tehran's top security official to revive peace talks. Iran has received a letter from Vance, but it has not responded to it yet, Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported, adding that Tehran wants the US to meet its conditions and "any position that contradicts this framework is unacceptable." Oil prices could become even more volatile in the next couple of weeks due to Israel's recent elections and the US midterm elections on November 3, according to a Saxo Bank briefing on Thursday. The Danish bank said crude is expected to trade in a higher range of $70 to $90 a barrel even after the conflict ends, compared with a pre-war range of $60 to $70. SAUDI EXPORTS RISE Saudi Arabia's crude exports rose in October from September, two of three ship-tracking companies said, despite Iranian attacks on shipping in the Gulf and claims by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis of attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The US oil rig count, an indicator of future output, rose by two. US crude oil output increased in August, while demand for crude oil and petroleum products declined, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said in its Petroleum Supply Monthly report on Friday. Meanwhile, Libya's National Oil Corporation said an armed group shut a valve on Friday on the main Hamada crude oil pipeline, which links the Hamada field to the Zawiya refinery. It said the closure of the valve had halted the flow of about 15,000 barrels per day.

Source: Reuters

MEXICO CITY, Oct 30 : Formula One champion Lando Norris has a simple view of racing: If a teammate beats him then it means he needs to do a better job. The McLaren driver says also that he always blames himself first, never his equipment. "I don't know what else I'm going to say," the Briton said ahead of a Mexico City Grand Prix that is set to see Mercedes' Italian Kimi Antonelli succeed him as world champion and become the youngest driver, at 20, to take the title. Antonelli has eclipsed his own teammate George Russell with nine wins to three and is 123 points clear of the more experienced Briton, who has had an erratic season of highs and lows.

Mercedes have said the current car does not suit Russell's style while the 28-year-old says he is still searching for answers. NOT DONE A GOOD ENOUGH JOB "If my teammate beats me in a car, I've not done a good enough job," said Norris, last year's winner in Mexico City, when asked about the Mercedes situation, setting out his own philosophy. "I've never blamed my equipment. I always look at myself first, I always blame myself first." Norris said he and teammate Oscar Piastri, who is 67 points behind him in the standings, had found the car difficult to drive in Texas last weekend, but he still blamed himself for not putting together a perfect lap in the final phase of qualifying. "Even though some of it's not my fault because the car was so tricky, I still don't say the only reason I'm not P2 is because the car was tricky. I say because I didn't do a perfect job," he explained. "I can't stand losing to whoever ... so I will have to do whatever I can to be better ... even if the car suits Oscar more than me, I've got to change. I don't know what else you're meant to do. That's my job as a driver." "You need to learn how to adapt to different situations. And I can't speak for the others. Whatever they say is what they say ... the only excuse I would have if I got beat by my teammate is that I've not done a good enough job and the excuse can't be it (the car) doesn't suit me." Norris said that flexibility had been the key to his own success last season, having to adapt when Piastri appeared to be romping away with the title. "I had to change what I was comfy doing. I had to change my expectation, what felt good versus what didn't feel good ... it's not 'my way should be the way'," added Norris. "It's always like - OK, it's a new car. How do I get the most out of it. I've always thought of it that way, not 'my driving style is the best driving style, why is it not doing what I want?'" Russell said on Thursday that there were a "few factors with the cars this year that potentially favour or hinder a certain driving style". He explained that he had always been on the throttle earlier than most on the exit to corners, which was not the most efficient way to drive with the new power units, and higher tyre pressures had also had an impact. "This season I haven't lost it overnight," said Russell. "It's just the hit rate. It's like a baseball player, like hitting a home run or you're missing the ball."

BEIJING: China 's first carrier-based stealth reconnaissance and strike drone , the GJ-21, recently completed its first takeoff and landing on the Sichuan, the country's first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, state news agency Xinhua reported on Friday (Oct 30). The trial underscores Beijing's push to integrate drone technology into its military modernisation drive, a decades-long effort in which China has developed advanced warships, fighter jets, missiles and increasingly capable unmanned systems. Xinhua hailed the test as "a breakthrough in China 's amphibious assault ship programme" and said it signifies the navy's ability to operate fixed-wing stealth drone s from large naval platforms. GJ-21 first appeared at a military parade Beijing held last year to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War Two, where it displayed different types of weapons.

Oct 30 : Alliant Energy expects to sign contracts for about 1 gigawatt of additional data-center demand within six months, its finance chief said on Friday, as rising AI use and growing electrification push US power demand to record highs. The new load would add to the 3.4 GW that Alliant has already contracted with Alphabet's Google, Meta Platforms and Blackstone-backed QTS Data Centers. Earnings growth could exceed the company's 8 per cent target if capital spending rises further to support future load growth and other investment opportunities, Chief Financial Officer Robert Durian said on a post-earnings call. "We continue to work on what I'll call capital upside for different opportunities, including the additional load growth that we may see from the data center prospects that we have," Durian said.

NEW YORK, Oct 30 : The US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining artificial intelligence companies' corporate disclosures as investor worries mount over a potential AI bubble that may have been fueled by circular deals, the agency's enforcement director told Reuters on Friday.  Big Tech stocks sold off this week as companies disclosed they are burning through cash to fuel their AI expansion at a time when interest rates are rising, raising questions about the sustainability of AI spending. David Woodcock, who became SEC enforcement director in May, said the agency does not want to stand in the way of tech innovation, but that it is the agency's job to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks.  "Our principal concern is that people are making accurate disclosures about material information so that investors know what they're getting into," Woodcock said in an interview. "Enforcement is a very necessary piece of making sure people are doing that."

Where such disclosure does not happen, "then enforcement will be present," he said. Woodcock also said that AI and superintelligence have made scams much easier and cheaper to manufacture at scale, raising risks for more and more people. Brokers and other firms need to have processes in place to protect retail investors and "take thoughtful action," he said. PRIVATE MARKETS AND PREDICTION MARKETS Woodcock said the SEC will continue to look at issues in private markets, adding that the enforcement team's asset management unit is very focused on conflicts of interest and valuations. "When people don't make accurate disclosures, whether it's about valuations or whatever, then there is a role for enforcement," Woodcock said. "I think you'll see more activity in this space." Reuters previously reported the SEC was probing a type of private equity fund as part of the agency's broader interest in the opaque markets.  Woodcock said the SEC also has a role in overseeing prediction markets, which allow people to bet on real-world events, including sports, government policy announcements and elections. The markets, led by Polymarket and Kalshi, have surged in popularity over the past two years and have been pushing into US stocks. Such equity-linked prediction markets would traditionally fall under SEC jurisdiction.  Woodcock said the agency's enforcement staff are working with policy officials as well as the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which broadly oversees swap markets, to monitor and regulate the booming new markets. When asked about the possibility of bringing cases against firms that do not register with the agency, Woodcock said the agency does not want to regulate the new industry through enforcement actions.  "We want to be involved where it makes sense, but not in a way that crushes innovation," he said.

MADRID: Spain's transport minister on Friday (Oct 30) rejected calls for his resignation over the second train accident on his watch to cause mass casualties this year, as authorities worked to identify the victims from a crash that killed at least 69 people. Lawmakers from across the political spectrum this week condemned Transport Minister Oscar Puente for attributing Wednesday's crash to a break in protocol by control centre operators rather than accepting responsibility, with rail workers' unions calling for his immediate dismissal. The crash, which happened near the town of Urda in central Spain, followed another accident involving the same rail companies on the same line that killed 46 people in January. It has reopened a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain's high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe, as the country prepares for an election that left-leaning Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has called for Nov 29.

"My duty now is not to focus on discussing whether I will remain in office, but on solving the problem, determining exactly what happened and providing clear explanations," Puente said at a press conference on Friday. At the scene of the crash, large cranes were lifting the mangled wreckage as the Civil Guard listed 64 people as missing in what is already Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013. It was unclear if all those missing were accounted for in the death toll. Authorities have carried out 49 autopsies so far and formally identified five people, three women and two men, Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on state television network TVE.

Cranes lift wrecked train carriages as rescuers search for victims following a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, Thursday, Oct 29, 2026. (Photo: AP/Manu Fernandez)

AUTHORITIES CAN'T RULE OUT MORE FATALITIES No additional bodies were found when rescue teams overturned a train carriage on Thursday, Castilla-La Mancha regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said on TVE. Identifying the bodies was proving difficult because many were in pieces, he said. On Thursday, rescue teams had placed partial remains in 31 bags. "We cannot rule out the possibility of more fatalities," Garcia-Page said. The collision occurred after several trains were automatically stopped due to the failure of a signalling system, after which the central control centre in Madrid took over. A train operated by state-owned Renfe was authorised to proceed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, according to Puente. Audio of communications between the control centre and the train drivers obtained by El Pais showed how a controller authorised the Renfe train to continue on its journey at a normal speed, which Puente said disregarded a protocol to travel at no more than 40 kph in such circumstances.

CONTROLLERS SAY FOCUS SHOULD BE ON FAILED SIGNAL SYSTEM The debate about who was at fault intensified, with unions saying it was unfair to lay the blame on human error. Raquel Ayllon, a union leader at state-owned infrastructure operator Adif, said controllers were having to operate under difficult working conditions. "Human error is being criticised and questioned very quickly, while people are not really focusing on the central issue: the failure of the safety system," Ayllon said on TVE. Puente said the number of staff working at the control centre in Madrid had almost doubled since 2012 and that the controller who made the call had been working for two hours when the crash occurred. "I have never used the term 'human error', although that is not to say that there was no human error," he said. He said the LZB train control system that failed on Wednesday had an average of 170 failures per year, which was about the same as the rest of Europe. The system was behind schedule for an upgrade, public documents show.

The European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) has been installed across most of Spanish high-speed rail, according to a factsheet by European rail association UNIFE, which developed the new standard. Thales España, the Spanish arm of the French equipment maker, won a 2021 contract to install the ERTMS on the Madrid-Seville line, site of the two fatal crashes, by early 2026, but the work fell behind and passed to Hitachi Rail in 2024, according to Thales. Thales declined to comment on the delay of the rollout. Puente said the ERTMS system on the Madrid-Seville line was expected to begin working in early 2027, adding that the delay was due to the complexity of installing the system while keeping the line in operation.

In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every state and US territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over the platforms’ harm to teens and agreed to make changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for teens. Oct 30 : The biggest US technology companies generated record amounts of cash in the first nine months of 2026, yet returned the smallest share of it to shareholders in at least 15 years as surging artificial intelligence spending squeezed share buybacks. The retreat threatens a long-standing source of support for technology share prices. With companies buying back fewer shares, investors are increasingly dependent on heavy AI investments delivering enough profit growth to justify their valuations. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle returned 9.3 per cent of the cash their businesses generated as dividends and buybacks in the first three quarters of the year, down from 27.4 per cent a year earlier, a Reuters analysis of LSEG data and companies' financial reports showed. Operating cash flow actually rose 29 per cent from a year earlier to a record $542.9 billion.

But capital spending, driven by the AI boom, doubled to $556.9 billion, exceeding the cash the five firms generated for the first time in data going back to 2011. That left them with a combined free cash flow deficit of $14 billion, against a surplus of $143.5 billion a year earlier. The squeeze has hit buybacks hardest. The five companies cut repurchases 83 per cent to $13.6 billion, from $81.8 billion a year earlier. BUYBACKS FIRST TO GO Dividends, which investors treat as a commitment, rose to $37 billion in the first nine months of 2026 from $33.9 billion a year earlier. Buybacks almost disappeared. Alphabet and Meta have not repurchased a share in 2026, after buying back $66.5 billion in the first nine months of last year. Amazon pays no dividend and has not bought back shares since 2022. Microsoft accounted for nearly all the five companies’ remaining repurchases, and cut its buybacks to $4.4 billion in the September quarter from $5.7 billion a year earlier. Some companies are no longer covering their payouts from what their businesses earn after capital spending. With combined free cash flow (FCF) negative, the five companies’ $50.6 billion in payouts was effectively funded from cash reserves, borrowing or share sales. Amazon’s capital spending of $75.9 billion in the third quarter was almost 80 per cent more than the $42.4 billion its operations generated, and it raised $48.1 billion of long-term debt in the quarter. Alphabet’s free cash flow was also negative, and it raised about $12.4 billion from share sales and $29 billion from debt. THE HIDDEN COST The loss of buybacks matters more than the dollar figures suggest, because buybacks have flattered per-share earnings for years. When companies buy back and retire their own shares, profits are spread across fewer shares, lifting earnings per share even when total profits do not grow. Alphabet reduced its share count by 9.5 per cent between the end of 2020 and 2025 through buybacks, ING said. That alone provided a boost of roughly 2 per cent a year to earnings per share (EPS), even without any increase in profits. Without that boost, per-share earnings must come from actual profit growth. That is a harder test, and it arrives just as depreciation charges on new data centres start to rise. It also lands where investors are most sensitive. Investors care “so much more about EPS than FCF,” Mark Schilsky, a technology sector specialist at JPMorgan, said in a client note last week. Technology and communication services stocks, which account for about 43.5 per cent of US market value, delivered a shareholder yield of just 0.28 per cent in July, against 1.99 per cent for the rest of the market, MSCI found. NO END IN SIGHT Amazon said it still expects about $220 billion of capital spending this year, and the other companies have signalled further increases. That leaves Big Tech shareholders with a different bargain from the one they signed up for, accepting less cash today in exchange for a bet that AI will eventually generate enough profit to make up for it. "For the last 15 years, companies increasingly returned excess capital to shareholders through buybacks and dividends," said Ehren Stanhope, co-head of investment management at Franklin Templeton. "The current regime may increasingly be characterized by greater equity and debt issuance, a request of capital from investors."

The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. The prospect of ever-bigger AI outlays has unnerved investors, particularly as rising borrowing costs threaten to make debt-funded investment more expensive and harder to justify. Here's a roundup of megacap earnings so far, with Apple set to report next week and AI bellwether Nvidia due mid-November. TECH WIPEOUT Alphabet suffered its biggest one-day percentage drop on record on Thursday after disappointing results in the core business of search advertising and a massive acceleration in cash burn. Meta's plans for a record $97.5 billion fund raise heightened concerns about shareholder dilution and whether mounting AI spending could force other Big Tech companies to increasingly tap capital markets. Microsoft and SpaceX broke from the gloom, with results that showed AI spending starting to pay off. "It may be that we've overestimated how strong the growth might be, but they're not going negative in aggregate," said John Bilton, global head of strategic research, multi-asset solutions at JPMorgan Asset Management. "We have an insatiable and growing demand for data." RISING DEBT PILE Microsoft is reportedly planning to raise about $25 billion through its first US investment-grade bond sale in more than nine years. Among other hyperscalers, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet have issued hundreds of billions of dollars in bond sales over the past four years, worrying investors about overreliance on the medium for raising capital. Morgan Stanley forecast capital spending on AI infrastructure overall will surpass a trillion dollars next year. COST TO INSURE AGAINST DEBT DEFAULT SURGE AI companies’ growing reliance on debt funding is emerging as a new risk for investors, challenging the view that the companies at the heart of the boom are insulated from macroeconomic pressures. The concern is spreading beyond stocks to credit markets, where investors are starting to price in the possibility that rising financing costs, combined with slower returns on AI spending, could squeeze companies previously viewed as relatively insulated. ROBUST REVENUE Revenue across the "Magnificent Seven" has remained strong since ChatGPT's launch in 2022, showcasing insatiable demand and perhaps why investors were initially willing to back the spending, even as the timeline of payoffs remains uncertain. Amazon's cloud computing cash cow, Amazon Web Services, continued to accelerate, while Meta offered better-than-expected revenue growth and an upbeat outlook. Microsoft also forecast strong cloud growth in its latest earnings report. SOARING CAPEX Big Tech has historically spent heavily on infrastructure to build and expand businesses such as cloud computing, online advertising and e-commerce, but the AI boom has pushed capital expenditure to dizzying levels. J.P. Morgan expects global AI capex to reach $5.5 trillion by 2030, and sees $900 billion being spent in 2026 alone. This year's AI capex by Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and Microsoft would likely equal their cumulative spend since the November 2022 launch of ChatGPT, J.P. Morgan analysts noted.
